The virus Phi X-174 (by the way, the "X" is the Roman numeral 10) has a long history in genomics because of its small genome size. Frederick Sanger and colleagues at the MRC in Cambridge England developed an ingenious but difficult method for sequencing DNA and in a tour de force publication in the journal Nature in 1977 presented its complete genome sequence (~5000 bases) .  A few weeks after it was published, I saw Sanger give a talk on it, and it was the closest to a standing ovation I've ever seen for a scientific talk. We knew a revolution in biology had begun. 
Sanger had already won a Nobel Prize in 1958 for developing methods for sequencing proteins, and won another in 1980 for DNA sequencing. Eventually Sanger's group made improvements in the sequencing methodology and the first bacterial genome sequence (ca. 1.8 million base pairs) was published in 1995. Eventually automated sequencing machines were developed and improved and a draft human genome sequence (ca. 3 billion base pairs) was published in 2000. Now any lab can obtain billions of bases of raw DNA sequence; however, it all started with PhiX174.

The Rhine River has never been all that easy a river to navigate without some adjustments.    At only a bit under 800 miles in its full corrected length, it has been subject to major difficulties to make it relatively easily traveled. 

The Rhine still requires at least a lock system as used in the panama canal to create the more easy travel along the river.    From 1817 a large reengineering project had to be started to remove a hairpin curve from the river which was not at all likely to see good passage possible, this being the Tulla Project.   Beyond that, the River had areas of rather limited depth which had to be dredged out and many areas saw the need to remove river bed deposits of large boulders which created a hazard for commercial craft travel. 
Much of this is to be found described in detail in MarK Cioc's work, The Rhine: an Eco-Biography 1815-2000, Seattle: U. Washington Press c. 2002 
The river is a major commercial and tourist artery for at least 5 Nations [Switzerland, France, Germany, Belgium and the Netherlands].
It is clearly now under threat!

The precise use of language is very important to me, but I can't get excited about "scam." Every natural language exists in tension between rules that define how the most powerful people of that tradition spoke one or two or five hundred years earlier, and popular usage, which is in constant flux. Most changes in popular usage are forgotten when the generation that invented them dies off. A few persist and become accepted usage. Then "the rules" must change to explain why they are natural and right.

True, the new uses of "scam" skip over defining exactly what is a scam: "[Today's atmosphere of alarm over the dangers of drinking] alcohol is a scam." English has always done that. "Jane drinks excessively." Drinks what... water, soda pop, Red Bull? Custom tells us that "drinks" without an object usually refers to alcohol.

So I consider the diatribe against "scam" a bit of column filler; sound and fury signifying nothing. In a generation this use of "scam" will probably be remembered, if at all, as quaint. Maybe, just maybe, it will become accepted usage, and people will wonder how it could ever have been different. In either case the world will survive, or not, regardless.

The challenge that has created is that a lot of small SaaS companies solve one business problem.  When they get to mid-size they try to add some adjacent solutions solving for other related pain points, but most customers are still only using it for the original problem.  Highly targeted  solutions are very often very easy to fix with vibe coding a tool or using AI because the requirements are easy to describe to AI. comments.name: Gary Wilmot
comments.body:
I am (thankfully) recently retired from 40+ years in the Product Lifecycle Management (PLM) software industry, which is now the poster-boy for the scenarios described in this article. It was no more than 5 years ago my previous employer, one of the recognized leaders in the industry, underwent a dramatic shift from Client/Server architecture to SaaS. Trust me, it was brutally painful for both the company and our customers, but also made total sense in the pre-ChatGPT world. I am not going to miss one bit not being there for this next “transformation”.

While being, for the most part, spot-on, this article overlooks one of the most critical challenges organizations face in implementing Enterprise level software systems - Regulatory Compliance. Companies operating under FDA, FAA, FCC, NHTSA, EPA and myriads of other regulations spend enormous amounts of software implementation budgets and time ensuring that the software system itself and the massive amount of product data it creates and manages complies with countless growing and changing regulations. One area you might think is relatively straightforward, but isn’t, is access control - literally, who can access what data in the system, from searching, viewing, creating and updating perspectives. Users may have access to some product data in the context of one product/project but be restricted from it completely in the context of another. Now layer on top of that the need to also restrict data access based on on what stage of Design/Development/Production the design is currently in, who the specific customer for the product is, even things like which geographic office location the same employee is currently logging in from. Got all that? Great, now recreate ALL of it to manage outside users from partners and subcontractors. . . you see the issue. The fact that current Enterprise systems are somewhat restrictive by design is actually a benefit in these scenarios.

The point is this - you can write all the slick, money-saving, time-slashing AI prompts you want to, but in these types of companies you’re not going to be doling any of them out to users until you can certify, beyond any doubt, that the agent isn’t going to violate a single one of the access control safeguards you spent months or years implementing, debugging and certifying. Like I said, I’m not going to miss being involved in those battles one bit.

Winning a Democratic primary does not necessarily demonstrate statewide electability. El-Sayed successfully mobilized progressive and anti-establishment voters, but Michigan’s general electorate includes independents, suburban moderates, and ticket-splitting voters who could respond differently. 

His positions on Israel/Gaza, progressive economic policies, and associations with controversial figures give Republican Mike Rogers opportunities to portray him as outside the political mainstream. 

At the same time, interpreting his victory purely as ideological would be a mistake: voters may have been rejecting establishment politics and heavy outside spending rather than endorsing the entire progressive agenda. El-Sayed’s economic-populist message could potentially reach voters beyond the Democratic base. 

The real November question is whether he can broaden his anti-establishment coalition into a statewide economic-populist movement. If the campaign instead becomes a referendum on progressive ideology and cultural issues, Republicans likely gain the advantage.

comments.name: Brita Wood
comments.body:
As resident of nearby Nelson, over the decades I have observed the influx of festival goers come into town to stock up on provisions for this annual festival. We also see them return afterwards trying to regain their equilibrium after a weekend of drug use and lack of sleep. 

In addition to this year’s 600 to 800 medical emergencies over the weekend cited in your article, attendees put others at risk by their driving behaviours. 

BC Highway Patrol maintained two roadblocks at the end of the festival, which resulted in the following:

311 tickets for speeding,

57 vehicles towed for mechanical safety or driver impairment,

51 24-hour driving suspensions for drug impairment,

85 Standardized Field Sobriety Tests for suspected drug-impaired driving,

30 Drug Recognition Expert evaluations resulting in 27 impaired-by-drug investigations and 23 blood draws by a lab technician,

50 violation tickets for a variety of BC MVA offences,

8 vehicles immediately removed from the road due to major mechanical defects.

Hundreds of violation tickets including 11 for no insurance. 

“We asked people before the event to make sure they allowed drugs to clear their system before driving, but too many ignored that advice,” Sgt. McLaughlin said. “It looks like we will have to be back next year, and hopefully in greater numbers, to deal with festival-goers who are driving unsafely.”

This is why so many commenters see the COS as the gatekeeper. comments.body:
Japan’s urban population grew from roughly 59 million in 1960 to a peak of about 115 million in the 2010s, and now sits at approx. 113.9 million. The proportion living in cities has reached an all-time high of over 92%.
Post-War Industrial Boom (1950–1979)
***1950: Urban areas comprise roughly 37% of the total national population.
***1960: World Bank data notes urban population is 63% of the total. 
Modern Urbanization and Peak (1980–2010)
***1990: Greater Tokyo continues upward, absorbing over 30% of total demographic footprint.
***2010: Census reports 90.7% of population lives in urban areas
Recent Decline (2011–Present)
***2011–2020: Population contraction; urban percentage climbs as rural towns shrink.
***2022–2026: The percentage of urban dwellers: ~92.1%.
---------------

many people would move out of cities and resettle the rural areas.  Housing prices

comments.name: Liz
comments.body:
Hello Hannah Beech & Kiuko Notoya,
Thank you for this article.  I see several human centered opportunities here that might be worth passing along to your contacts.  First, there’s a little program available called WWOOF (Willing Workers On Organic Farms), that connects workers (generally young, dedicated international travelers) with local farmers for week to multi month agricultural work performed in exchange for room and board.  Hosts receive labor and a bit of cultural exchange while avoiding long term residence that might fuel concerns for cultural dilution. Farmers in my PNW region use this organization to run their small operations with pretty fair results!  
Second, there are dozens of former federal employees available who have extensive experience working with hazard and nuisance animals (including habituated bears), who would probably be delighted by the opportunity to work in Japan adjusting the behaviors of these animals.  These people are friendly, well trained and professional, and are likely currently underutilized.  Could be an effective and mutually beneficial solution!  
Best regards and thanks for a great article.

The markets may put a good deal too much trust in President Trump and his statements or the nature of the speculation as to what 'the Fed' may do in the near future as has been generally voiced by its Chairman.    If that is not ideal, it is the reality with which we see as the general practice and that is hard to see as at all 'turning on the dime'.

If Kevin Warsh wants to avoid his own useful address of some general forecast, the market will not generally drop its own ideas of some prognostication.    The market, in its nature, seeks to look to indicators for a future's course.    The market would use the nature of LIBOR or some other interest rate as an indicator for banking and mortgage rates and the financial influences to be then applied to other aspects of the market functioning.

The lack of Kevin Warsh's concerns may see his presentations less useful to the market needs, but it will hardly see the market ignoring any attempt at prognostication.   The market will simply make its own assumptions as to the nature of its predictions using whatever surrogate materials they can manage.

Someone loses a case as between the employee and the union, or as between an employer and a union, and the loser appeals like any court decision can be appealed.  That fact hearing is over and the appeal goes up on the established record.  

If you're saying the original fact hearing did not afford due process, that's one thing and certainly is a legitimate position, I've had the same issue on that for years.  And if you're saying that the investigative and hearing processes should not be within the same agency, I certainly agree with that, they all work in the same offices and are buddies.  And do these agencies function as advocates?  Yes, they certainly do, and in the labor context it is usually in favor of the union whether the other party was a member or an employer.  

So I'm kind of confused on what your point is?  If agencies, labor or otherwise, can't defend a hearing officer's or ALJ's decision, then are you saying they don't get to particpate in appeals of their own decisions and the state agency should defer to  winning party to defend the agency? comments.name: C Christy
comments.body: Steven Foukal, the "digital wellness entrepreneur" quoted here, left Thailand for Vietnam because, in his words, "more and more people want an escape." That sentence is the whole psychology of this migration: a country with a war, a French occupation, and a legal system built partly to punish the vices colonizers once used to pacify it, treated as a cheaper backdrop for content once Bangkok tightened its visa rules. A Da Nang resident says his quiet block got rezoned for nightlife four years ago, and he now opens his door most mornings to drunks asleep on the pavement. Nobody arriving is reading up on Vietnamese history, they're doing visa arbitrage: Cambodia cracked down on scam compounds, Thailand shortened its visa window, so both the nomads and the fraud rings moved next door. A man rips his shirt off and chokes a stranger, and the coverage pivots to how harsh Vietnam's courts are rather than to why a country this affordable keeps absorbing people this entitled. The Disneyland instinct doesn't stop at the ticket booth. It just goes looking for the cheapest one.

comments.name: R C
comments.body:
I went to Vietnam over twenty years ago to visit the Vietnamese relatives of my cousins. It was an interesting experience. By and large the young Viet people spoke reasonably good English, were welcoming and lamented that much of the world still perceived their country as a communist hellhole. Many had completed university education in hospitality and were worried they would have to find work abroad.

It was, at that time, fairly uncrowded and it wasn't difficult to do pretty much anything you wanted. I definitely enjoyed it more than Thailand and while I would later discover that traveling into the highlands is the right way to visit Thailand, back then you were still mostly encouraged not to go north of Bangkok.

Western attitudes towards criminality don't work even for the non-communist East and Southeast Asian states. We tend to view criminal behavior as a personal failing, while in those cultures it is typically viewed as a familial failing. When the state is forced to intervene, its intent is to send a message to the entire family to handle their own business going forward.

Honestly, Mr. Lilly knew he was doing something wrong. He didn't take required medication because he was depressed and he spiraled. The consequences are, on this occasion, harsh but they aren't unwarranted. If you burn your neighbor's house down, you shouldn't expect leniency.

Here's a take on Puerto Rican politics that seems not to have made it in the letters advocating statehood or independence.

The first elected governor, Luis Muñoz Marín, established an extremely popular government that made dramatic improvements in living conditions. He tried taking the status issue off the table by dressing up colonialism as a "Free Associated State". 

The 1% realized they would never win elections against this commie government and argued for statehood on the grounds it was undignified to be a state and managed to make wedge issue politically important, as it remains even today. To be fair, Muñoz' successors in his party did not have his political savvy and some were corrupt.

To improve the well-being of borinqueños, the political scene needs to ignore the status issue, over which the island has no control (the US Congress will never permit either independence or statehood), and focus attention on the island's myriad problems, this water disaster being one of many. If you look at the long term graph of 10 year bond yields they rarely dipped below 5% prior to 2005 and were largely above 6 or 7% in the 80’s and 90’s. 

The economy did just fine other than in the mid 70’s when high rates and the Arab Oil embargo tested the U.S. economy. Since 2005 when Greenspan printed scads of money to get rates  to 2% (some would say artificially), pressures on the economy resulting from the 2010 Great Recession and then COVID have kept rates low to stimulate recovery. 

Now that we’re past these constraints but facing problematic but less onerous ones such as heavy tariffs, a dwindling immigrant  workforce and dumb wars, rates are naturally resetting towards pre-2005 levels. Perhaps higher rates and their dampening effect on borrowing for A.I. might just be a good thing; a natural market antidote to A.I. “irrational exuberance” (to quote Greenspan).

comments.name: capillary
comments.body: TIPS (treasury inflation protected securities) are a permutation of treasury bonds that are worth considering in an inflationary environment.  with TIPS the principal value of the bond is adjusted twice a year over and above the coupon rate of the bond by the U.S. Dept. of the Treasury based on the consumer price index (CPI-U).  in an inflationary environment this means that the principal value of the bond increases, (which also enhances the interest paid by the bond).  TIPS have certain tax advantages in tax-free and tax-deferred retirement accounts, but can also be useful outside of such accounts.  furthermore, the coupon rate of TIPS tends to be lower than fixed rate treasuries, but in a volatile inflationary environment they can provide significant protection to investors.

The rains usually start in October and last until the end of May. Around November it gets cold enough that the rains turn into snow and build the snowpack for the summer. Not this year. It didn’t get cold enough in the mountains so all that rain rushed down the mountains and created some of the worst flooding on record. The ski resorts suffered. They could barely keep them open. I knew that the 2026 summer would be horrible. We still have about 3 months to go before the rains come again. Global warming is real.

I’m in Portland. I have asthma. I’m running two HEPA air filters full blast in my apartment. It sounds like an airport jetway. For the last two days I could feel ashes in my mouth even with the filters running. Lots of hits on the rescue inhaler, and I’m alternating between an N95 and a P100 respirator when I have to go outside (and sometimes inside, too). Hard to sleep through the night. It’s exhausting. 

I need to leave here for my health but I am stuck in my job until I retire, assuming there’s anything left to retire from by then. I’m worried the safe places will be overrun by the wealthy by the time I can go. 

I feel guilty complaining about my first-world problems. I can’t help but worry about the homeless folks in my neighborhood. Many of them are in very poor health and many of them won’t accept help. 

The smoke is dissipating for now and the particulates are starting to clear here. We still have an ozone alert until tomorrow evening, assuming they don’t extend it again. 

People are tired and stressed. There is also a band down the street playing music outside.

I only wish I had such resources when my mom, aunts,  uncles and grandparents were alive to share at past reunions.  It was fascinating how much I learned from small town newspapers in South Central Kansas. I learned how frequently my mom’s father traveled to find work, and how my father’s parents, both born around 1890, met.  I was surprised to discover that my paternal grandmother’s father abandoned his family and ran off to Oregon after selling cattle that a bank had loan him money to buy - something she never told me after her son, my father, left my mom and moved to Oregon too.  Or that my dad’s eventual second wife’s then husband shot himself dead at the doorway of his girlfriend’s apartment after she dumped him — his wife at the time was living with my father.  

These newspapers also had what could be considered gossip columnists, whose writings could be cruel.  I never knew my mom’s grandfather left my great-grandmother, twice, with the small newspaper noting after the final time that she had “moved back in with her son — again.”  I thought the dysfunction in my family only began after I was born.

There's a lot of talk about robots replacing us, i.e., as a species, which is purely science fiction. 

One of the things about robots is that they are extremely high-maintenance devices, and require highly-skilled people with a panoply of skills to design, build and repair them. Just think of the organisational nous necessary to run the business, to project-manage the design, the supply chain coordination to purchase the parts and materials necessary to manufacture the robots, the complex machinery to assemble them, and when one fails (in hardware and/or software) the ability to diagnose and fix the problem, to disassemble, replace parts, reassemble. Even in science fiction movies it's still humans doing all that work. We can always just keep them away from electrical outlets, not charge their batteries.

It might also be noted that "autonomy" is an important word here: much of the hype, such as the recent dancing robots video from China, even those marketing videos from Boston Dynamics, are either preprogrammed routines or remote-controlled by humans, they're not demonstrations of creative, autonomous choreography any more than are night-time drone "fireworks" displays, i.e., impressive in their own right, but hardly anything to worry about as some kind of nascent, silicon-based species.

In many parts of rural Canadian (Northern Ontario, Maritimes & BC interior to name a few) it’s jokingly referred to as the Canadian dinner jacket. Every Canadian young adult or teenager at some point in their lives had one as they continue to have eras as fashion requirements along with other uniquely Canadian clothing items. In my teens having one and either a pair of Mukluks or Kodiak boots (laces loose of course) was non negotiable. comments.body: Our first Safari was in Tanzania in early November when we were lucky not to encounter any rains. It was absolutely magical our first afternoon in in Tarangere National Park. We went down to the river and saw Lions, elephants and many other animals. For Tanzania, I highly recommend a local agent. If you go to TripAdvisor, you will see a list of recommended operators. Our second was in late February early March where the migration was in Indutu just south of Serengeti. We saw millions of animals there. It was a little bit late for the calving that year but we saw many, many young wildebeest and cheetahs and lions on the hunt. We are heading out in a few days for another adventure this time. Even the best behaved children do not have the attention span needed for a day of wildlife watching - they get restless, bored, sleepy, whiny or over stimulated. comments.body:
As a former international teacher based for 5 years in Abuja, I traveled during school breaks to Cape Town, Nairobi, and other classic safari destinations.

If a safari is your main goal, this article's advice is fine.  

I'd suggest there's much more to see across Africa, and keep in mind you're most likely visiting 1 or maybe 2 or 3 of the continent's 50 odd nations: there's much you'll end up missing no matter what.  

I like Cape Town and Stellenbosch, one of the nearby wine regions with its own beauty, hiking, and nearby beaches.  It's a fine introduction to Africa, but the recent unrest against immigrants would make me hesitate.  

Kenya is well worth exploring too, although I found it more effective to skip the overpriced tourist sites, and work with a local to see more hidden spots, like caves and former guerilla camps from the Mau-Mau uprising that preceded independence there.  

Nigeria's security makes travel within the nation difficult, but Yankari, West Africa's oldest wildlife preserve, is worth the effort.  It's a day's drive from the capital, in Bauchi state.  Nok village is closer, in Kaduna, as are other cultural attractions.  

My advice would be to research ahead of time and then chose a destination, making the safari part of a more extensive exploration of your chosen destination.  

Consider avoiding the best known spots: Uganda instead of Rwanda for gorillas.  It'll save a lot.  

See the people, talk to them.  Learn from them.  Then decide what to do.

comments.name: culturejamming-M LeVine
comments.body:
Wow! An entire article on country music in Africa, and not a single mention that country music is in good measure from Africa. The banjo is an African instrument. Versions of the violin and the guitar have existed in Africa for thousands of year. The origins of country music in the US lie in the deep south, with the field hollers and songs of the African slaves and their descendants, which then mixed together with Irish, cajun and Indigenous musics to create the genre we all know. Even the country twang has direct African roots. Indeed, it wasn't called "country" till it was raced in the 1920s and black and white artists were separated. 

But for Africans who started hearing country music almost as soon as the first records hit the Continent not long after the genre emerged, it just sounded like home. And yes, Africans have lots of "cowboys" and they don't just were stetsons. Polo is very big in Nigeria, Kenya and across Africa as well. 

Watch "Sinners" or watch Ken Burns' "Country Music" and you'll learn the same thing - country music is indelibly African, so returning home is no different than hip hop or blues or rock or jazz becoming hugely popular across sub-Saharan Africa.

comments.body: My father was a marine in the 6th Division, survived the horrors of Okinawa and  was preparing  himself for more slaughter in the invasion of Japan when it was announced that Japan had suddenly surrendered after the atomic bombs had been dropped. My mother's brother, on the other hand, tool a different course.  His naval unit had been subjected to Kamikaze attacks off the Philippines and then faced even more intense fire off Okinawa. He too was to be involved in the initial invasion of the mainland of Japan when the war suddenly ended. However his initial enthusiasm for the atomic bombings changed after he was posted  in the occupation force to a hospital near Hiroshima which  treated hundreds of  burned and maimed children. comments.name: Kando
comments.body:
As a former historian of Japan (now retired) who taught courses on the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, I first believed as a historical fact that those bombings led directly to the end of the war. And I taught it that way for years.

However, every time I taught that course I dug deeper into the primary sources regarding the Japanese surrender, and could find no evidence that the atomic bombings were the primary concern of the Japanese high command. Rather, they saw them in the context of, for example, the incendiary bombing of Tokyo on the night of March 9-10, 1945, which also killed approximately 140,000 persons.

Any explanation of the Japanese surrender requires the inclusion of the Soviet declaration of war on Japan. The Soviets wanted badly to split Japan just as Germany had been split. The Japanese wanted to keep their country whole and knew that the Americans were as anti-Communist as they were. It was an advantage to the Japanese to surrender to the Americans, which they did on August 15, 1945. Nevertheless, the Soviets did not agree to a cease-fire until August 22.

comments.name: Joseph Appel
comments.body:
A footnote to this sobering find from Capt. Lewis’ personal record of the event: 

a few days ago, I read in veterantributes.org about 1st Lieutenant USAAF Jacob Beser, the radar countermeasures specialist who served on the Enola Gay as well as on the crew of Boxscar, the B-29 which carried out the atomic bombing of Nagasaki three days later. According to Veteran Tributes, Lieutenant Beser was the only crewmember who flew on both atomic bombing missions, which led virtually immediately to Japan’s surrender.  His name appears as one of three specialists listed on Capt. Lewis’ notepad. No matter what our opinions are about the worthiness of atomic energy as a legitimate military tool, we’ve got to reckon the weight of the actions of these crew members and hopefully the gravitas they carried with them forever after.

Of course, today is the anniversary of Hiroshima. Reading these articles got me thinking about nuclear weapons and especially the risks they present to the survival of all life on Earth, and Earth itself. We Americans need to place this issue front and center in our politics as the United States now promotes nuclear proliferation in the Middle East even as it professes to limit it.

Joseph Appel
Woodstock, NY

I don't live in the Barbican or in fact London but I must say that I wholeheartedly opposed the One Silk Street project from the outset and continue to do so.

I agree with Trevor Kavanagh's (one of our generation's most outstanding journalistic voices) sentiment that the residents' light will become "obliterated" due to this development- in fact, the rays of the Sun may no longer reach the balconies of the Barbican at all. To make matters worse, the aesthetic coherence of the complex, the harmonious unity of design elements which make the Barbican unique, will die a slow death as the Silk Street monstrosity casts its shadow over the area.

I have spoken with many Barbican residents who share similar fears and also believe that the additional foot traffic resulting from this development will contribute to an increase in antisocial behavior, such as parkour, skateboarding, and "stunts," which is already at unacceptable levels.

I offer my full solidarity to the Barbican residents during this trying time, and hope that any and all legal avenues to prevent this development occuring are pursued.

Peet was for many years a Disney animator, joining the studio in the late 1930s to work on “Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs”, and remaining there till the early 1960s. He focused on writing and illustrating children’s books after leaving animation.

“Capyboppy” is based on his family’s adoption of a young capybara (in an era when trade in exotic pets was less regulated than it is now); the title is the name they gave their new pet. It was generally an amiable addition to the family, but they ultimately had to keep it outside at night, since, like all rodents, it chewed constantly, and the huge critter would destroy their furniture if left unsupervised.

This exclusion from the family, however, distressed the capybara, a highly social animal. Capyboppy became moody and erratic. comments.name: N.G. Krishnan

​This strategic agreement feels straight out of Aesop’s fable of The Frog and the Mouse—where two uneasy allies tie themselves together for mutual protection, only to find that tethering disparate, vulnerable bodies together in turbulent waters usually ends up dragging everyone down under the eyes of the hawk.

​The sheer tragedy of this treaty lies in its desperation. You have a cash-flush Gulf monarchy looking for hard power and potential nuclear insurance, a nuclear-armed state plagued by chronic economic collapse, and a NATO member balancing its own regional ambitions—all trying to construct a cohesive defense shield out of fundamentally conflicting priorities.

​When you treat an attack on one as an attack on all in a region overflowing with volatile rivalries, a minor flare-up on one front risks dragging all three into a catastrophic spiral nobody actually wants. 

It’s a classic geopolitical tragedy: an alliance born to manufacture stability through collective deterrence, but so structurally fragile that it might instead guarantee shared ruin.

comments.name: Thomas Radke
comments.body: A personal note to Mr. Barker. I too was involved in an airplane incident which I survived (obviously) and after which I vowed never to fly again. I was flying back from a business trip from Peoria, Illinois with 9 coworkers and 2 pilots in an old twin engine Cessena. Over the border of Iowa and Minnesota we ran into a very bad storm front which threw our plane down towards the ground. We turned sideways and nose down. Everything not tied down inside the interior began to free float like in space. I actually ripped the arm rest completely off my seat. We all assumed that we were dead meat. Suddenly the engines were growling like an old Sky King TV show and we leveled out but as we we flying level just above the ground we were not out of trouble. Trees separating corn fields lay ahead and the pilots barely cleared them. We could hear the bottom of the plane hitting the top branches.  I turned in my seat and screamed at the pilots "what did you do"?; he replied that he'd thrown out the landing gear to find a way to level the plane. Smart thinking. When we landed I reached beneath the plane and pulled a long corn stalk out of a wheel assembly. We we literally that close to crashing. I couldn't keep my vow to never fly again as 2 weeks later we were all again on that same plane heading to Peoria. Besides, I wanted to fly back to Germany and that's a long boat ride. Don't give up on flying. It's very safe compared to other ways of traveling. If your time is up then it's up.
